18658-in-macao:
Charles A. Gunnison published this short tale at San Francisco in 1892, as a story from the Grasshopper's Library. It opens in a garden at Macao, near the grotto of the poet Camoens, where a Portuguese priest chatting with the narrator suddenly attacks his uncle Robert with a stiletto. The uncle fires his revolver, and the priest falls dead at the narrator's feet.

From that shock the tale turns to Macao itself, seen from a steamer out of Hong Kong as a bright crescent bay town under the Portuguese flag. Pink, blue, and yellow houses, forts, and Chinese junks fill the scene. The story mixes travel color with sudden violence in a far eastern port.
britannica-1911-bilbao:
Bilbao is the capital of the Spanish province of Biscay, in the north of Spain. It stands on the river Nervion, about eight miles inland from the Bay of Biscay. Its 1900 population was 83,306. The 1911 Britannica entry calls it one of Spain's chief seaports and the greatest of Basque towns. Mountains shut in its small, fertile valley on every side but the sea. Five bridges cross the river between old and new town.

The old town climbs in terraces on the right bank, the new town spreads on the left. San Antonio bridge, of stone, dates from the 14th century. Mining and metal work lead its industries, with breweries, tanneries, and flour mills behind. Don Pedro Lopez de Haro founded Bilbao about 1300. The Carlists besieged it in vain in 1835 and 1874. French troops held it from 1808 to 1813.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartholomeu-l:
Bartholomeu Lourenço de Gusmão was a naturalist and the first aeronaut, born at Santos, Brazil, in 1685, who died at Toledo in 1724. He left a Jesuit novitiate at Bahia in 1701, studied at Coimbra, and became Doctor of Canon Law. In 1709 he petitioned John V of Portugal for privilege over his airship invention, with great confidence. His design spread a huge sail over a bark, with bellows blowing air through tubes when wind failed.

Magnets in hollow metal balls were to propel it, though gases and hot air likely filled the shells instead. The public test set for 24 June 1709 never took place, but he made lesser experiments descending from heights. His contrivance embodied the kite's principle, and he also wrote on navigating the air and pumping leaking ships. Charged before the Inquisition on another matter, he fled to Spain and died of fever at Toledo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-curacao:
A mission entry covers Curacao, a vicariate apostolic embracing the Dutch West Indies: Curacao, Bonaire, and Aruba, plus Saba, St. Eustatius, and Dutch St. Martin. Discovered by Ojeda in 1499, the islands first heard Spanish Hieronymite missionaries from Santo Domingo. Spain held Curacao until 1634, when the Dutch West India Company banned Catholic practice under severe penalties.

Jesuits still worked in secret from 1701 to 1742. A first prefect apostolic came in 1772, Dutch Franciscans followed in 1776, and M. J. Nieuwindt, appointed prefect in 1824, became first vicar apostolic when the vicariate was erected in 1842. Dutch Dominicans took charge in 1868. Nine-tenths of the people were Catholics, served by churches, schools, hospitals, and two Catholic newspapers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-damao:
A diocesan entry describes Damao, a suffragan see of Goa in Portuguese India and the Bombay presidency, erected by Leo XIII in 1886 under a concordat settling Goa's claims against Propaganda. Dom Antonio Pedro da Costa, nominated by Portugal's king, took possession in June 1887, and the church of Bom Jesus became his cathedral.

The city, on the Arabian Sea about 100 miles north of Bombay, first met the Portuguese in 1523 when a storm drove Diogo de Mello into its harbour. Sacked in 1529, it heard its first Mass in 1541 and was finally secured in 1558 when its larger native garrison fled before 3,000 attackers. The diocese also held churches in Bombay itself, including Nossa Senhora da Gloria in Mazagon, the bishop's Bombay residence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fernando-cast:
Fernando Castro Palao was a Spanish Jesuit moral theologian famed for holy life and learning. Born at Leon in 1581, he entered the Jesuits in 1596. He taught at Valladolid, Compostella, and Salamanca: philosophy, moral theology, and theology in turn. He became rector at Medina and consultor of the Inquisition.

Students flocked in great numbers to his moral theology classes at Compostella. His decisions were treated as oracles on the hardest cases sent to him. His Opus Morale spans seven volumes on all moral theology. Alphonsus and Gury rank him among the chief guides on moral theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-macao:
Macao is a diocese suffragan of Goa, founded 23 January 1575 by Gregory XIII's bull, with its see in the Portuguese settlement on Heung-Shan island off Kwang-tung. Its name joins Ma, a local divinity, and gau, harbour, though Portugal preferred the grander City of the Holy Name of God of Macau.

Once prosperous, its trade was nearly killed by Hong Kong, founded forty miles east in 1842. Its jurisdiction first covered China and Japan entire, then shrank as Funay, Peking, Nanking, and Tonking were carved out, leaving Kwang-si, Kwang-tung, and later parts of Malacca, Singapore, and Portuguese Timor. Jesuits built here the colleges of St. Paul and St. Joseph, centres of Far Eastern mission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mattheus-pinn:
Born in Rio de Janeiro in 1687, Mattheus Pinna da Encarnacao became a Benedictine monk in 1703 and grew into the leading theologian of colonial Brazil. He studied at Rio and Bahia, took priestly orders in 1708, and taught philosophy and theology. His peers ranked him the most learned monk of his province, and he was widely loved for his care of the poor, the sick, and the overlooked.

Elected abbot at Rio in 1726, he clashed with the governor, was banished in 1727, fled to Portugal, and won his return through Cardinal Motta in 1729. He held the abbot's chair again at Rio and Bahia, twice served as provincial abbot, and in old age chose prayer over office. His books include a treatise on grace and free will, four volumes of Gospel sermons, and an unfinished six-volume dogmatic theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pharao:
Pharao was the title Scripture gives Egypt's ancient kings, and this Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces the word itself. It comes from Egyptian Per'o, great house, first the palace, then the government, then the ruler, much as Vatican or Quirinal stand for powers today. By the eighteenth dynasty it served as a reverent royal title, and from the twenty-fifth it commonly stood alone before the king's name.

Biblical usage mirrors Egyptian practice with fair accuracy: early kings appear under the bare title, while personal names arrive with the twenty-second dynasty. The entry then tests the title against the patriarchs, setting Joseph under a Hyksos king of the seventeenth century BC and weighing the Exodus against Merneptah's reign about 1225. Uncertain chronologies keep Abraham's pharaoh unnamed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-preto-ribeira:
Ribeirão Preto, raised on 7 June 1908, serves as a suffragan see under São Paulo's archdiocese in Brazil, with a Catholic flock of 500,000 souls. Its first and present bishop, Alberto José Gonçalves, was born on 20 July 1859, raised on 5 December 1908, and consecrated on 29 April 1909.  Its chief product is coffee, shipped in such bulk that trains must run without cease.

The see city, Ribeirão Preto, stands where Ribeirão Preto meets Ribeirão Retiro, 264 miles from the state capital. The municipality, made by a law of 1 April 1889, splits into four wards: Villa Tibeiro, Barracão, Morro do Cipó, and Republica. It boasts electric light and fine sewer and water works. Its streets run well laid, straight, and crossing at right angles, amid many parks and squares.  Schools and colleges abound, chief among them those kept by the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sao-luiz-de-m:
São Luiz de Maranhão, a Brazilian diocese suffragan of Belém do Pará, covers the state of Maranhão in the north. Its prefecture joined Olinda in 1614, and on 30 August 1677 it became a bishopric under Lisbon. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a see that once covered half a continent.

Antônio de Santa Maria, a Capuchin, was named first but moved to Miranda before taking possession, so Gregório dos Anjos, a canon of St John the Evangelist, became first bishop instead. At first the diocese held Maranhão, Pará, and Amazonas. Vacant from 1813 to 1820, it passed to São Salvador in 1827, lost Piauí in 1905, and joined Belém in 1906. It now counts 177,560 square miles, about 500,000 Catholics, fifty-seven parishes, and some hundred churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tuguegarao:
A diocese in the Philippines, in the north-eastern section of Luzon, embracing Cagayan, Isabela and Nueva Vizcaya with the Batanes and Babuyanes islands. Erected on 10 April 1910 from the ancient Diocese of Nueva Segovia, founded in 1595, it holds within its limits Lalloc, where Nueva Segovia's seat stood for two hundred years.

For three centuries before the Spanish-American War, the church history of the Cagayan Valley is largely the story of the Spanish Dominicans. The diocese counts 23 native secular priests, Spanish seculars and Dominicans, and Belgian missionaries, serving about 200,000 people, nearly all Catholics, under its first bishop, Maurice Patrick Foley.
podcast-dannyjones-qr1PFNRgOao:
Physicist David Chester joins Danny Jones to talk about UFO physics and a secret race toward anti-gravity. Chester works on the math of how such craft might fly. His talk stays close to fields, mass, and energy.

Chester lays out how anti-gravity might work if the reports of craft are true. He names the labs and states he thinks are in the race. Jones asks what a win in that race would mean for war and travel. Listeners with a taste for hard science get a dense talk. The library files it as an archive record.
podcast-dannyjones-wTNBhMZz2Ao:
Analyst Scott Horton joins Danny Jones to warn that the Pentagon is on red alert and Mossad has been named the top threat. The episode title quotes Horton's alarm. Horton is a writer and radio host known for anti-war work.

Horton lays out the clash he sees between US and Israeli spy aims. He argues the bond hides a deep spy war that now nears a break. Jones asks what proof backs the red alert claim. Listeners get a tense brief on a bond most press treats as iron. The library files the talk as an archive record of his stated view.
podcast-joerogan-ONV76ZfcPao:
Comedian Duncan Trussell joins Joe Rogan for episode 2247 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Trussell is a comic and mystic whose talks with Rogan are famed for their wild, warm roam. He hosts a show of his own with the same loose soul.

Trussell and Rogan drift from death and God to drugs, love, and the end of the world, laughing all the way. The talk has no map, and that is the charm his fans seek. Rogan plays the straight man to Trussell's cosmic riffs. Listeners get a long, strange hug of a talk. The library keeps the episode as a record of their bond.
podcast-joerogan-Rxmw9eizOAo:
Graham Hancock joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1284 to argue for a lost civilization. Hancock's books claim that an advanced culture fell at the end of the ice age and passed its knowledge to the ancient world. By this visit, the case was already a show staple.

He updates Rogan on the sites and finds he rates highest, from carved stone in Turkey to flood tales on every continent. Rogan asks how the experts answer, and Hancock gives his view of their blindness. The episode is a mid-arc statement of the theory that later reached a mass TV audience.
